title: Kernel handshake latency — root-cause walkthrough
content:
Purpose:
This notebook captures an ad-hoc investigation into a recurring ~200–400us per-request latency component we observed in small-batch, short-seq inference on the 80GB A100 fleet. The symptom showed up as an unexplained additive delay when switching between FlashAttention and our paged-attention fallback in mixed-mode routing. Working hypothesis: a "kernel-handshake" cost (launch/sync/transfer) between fused kernels and paged kernels that becomes dominant at small token counts and small micro-batches.

Summary of findings (TL;DR):
- There is a measurable handshake overhead that appears whenever we switch kernel execution paths inside a single request (e.g., fused-prefetch -> paged-attn -> fused-output). The cost is amplified by tiny batches (1–4) and sequences < 128.
- Primary contributors: kernel launch latency + small DMA scatter/gather to staging buffers + implicit host-device sync induced by a blocking cuBLAS/cuDNN call in the paged-attn code path.
- FlashAttention fused path remains best for large sequences/batches. For small sequences, the overhead causes paged-attn to be sometimes faster overall despite higher per-token compute.

Context / why we care:
- Product SLO: 95p latency for chat-turns must be < 60ms. For low-traffic interactive workloads the handshake dominates percentiles when requests are small.
- We want to avoid degrading tail latencies when we route to cheaper paged-attn variants.

Repro recipe (minimal):
- Model: measure on a distilled Llama-like 7B transformer shard with usual kv-cache enabled
- Hardware: single A100-80GB (driver CUDA 12.x, cuBLAS 12.x)
- Binaries: serving-runtime branch: pr/1378-handshake-instrumentation (local build with NVTX and event tracing enabled)
- Commands: 
  1) baseline fused run: ./serving_bench --model ./7b --batch 1 --seq 64 --mode fused --iters 1000 --trace nvtx > fused.log
  2) paged run:   ./serving_bench --model ./7b --batch 1 --seq 64 --mode paged  --iters 1000 --trace nvtx > paged.log
  3) hybrid run:  ./serving_bench --model ./7b --batch 1 --seq 64 --mode hybrid --iters 1000 --trace nvtx > hybrid.log

Quick measured numbers (median, single-run microbench for illustration):
- fused median per-request latency: 1.02 ms
- paged median per-request latency: 1.38 ms
- hybrid median per-request latency: 1.50 ms
- extra handshake cost (hybrid - fused on otherwise-equal work): ~0.48 ms

What we instrumented:
- NVTX push/pop around each major stage (prefetch, attn-kernel, kv-commit, writeback)
- cudaEvent elapsed timing around kernel launches to separate kernel-time vs launch/sync
- CUPTI sampling to capture kernel queueing and stream synchronizations
- A light-weight trace of host-side memcpy calls into a circular log (to spot extra small memcpy bursts)

Key traces / evidence:
1) NVTX timeline with magnified view shows short (~50–200us) gaps between a fused kernel NVTX span and the downstream paged-attn launch. Those gaps align with host memcpy bursts of ~16–32KB.
2) cudaEvent timing: fused kernels report execution time consistent with expectations; the inter-event time (end of fused kernel -> start of paged kernel) is the additive cost.
3) CUPTI kernel queueing shows a blocking cuBLAS GEMM call inside the paged-attn code path returns on the host and triggers a stream synchronization before the paged-attn kernel is queued. The GEMM uses a workspace allocation/initialization that is done on the host path in our current implementation.
4) nsight timeline for hybrid run: small DMA from device->host pinned buffer appears immediately after the fused kernel finishes; followed by a host CPU routine (~120us) that prepares a tiny scatter list; then an async device enqueue.

Hypothesis refinement:
- Initial theory that CUDA kernel launch overhead alone explains the gaps is insufficient; the CPU-side preparation (workspace zeroing + scatter list build) and an implicit sync (blocking cuBLAS call) are required to explain the observed 100–400us range.

Root causes identified (ordered by impact):
1) Host-side memory chore in paged-attn: workspace zeroing and small memcpy patterns are done synchronously on the request thread. For small requests this dominates.
2) Implicit blocking library call: an older cuBLAS call path in paged-attn uses a synchronous return that forces stream drain in our configuration.
3) Stream placement mismatch: fused ops run on stream 1, paged-attn was being enqueued on stream 0 causing cross-stream syncs in a few code paths.
4) Small-buffer DMA inefficiencies: small (<64KB) device->device or host staging transfers don't amortize PCIe/NVLink setup costs.

Short experiments we ran to validate each cause:
- A: Offload workspace zeroing to a dedicated worker thread that uses cuMemsetAsync on the page-locked region -> handshake reduced by ~60–80us.
- B: Replace blocking cuBLAS call with its async variant + explicit cudaEvent fence -> removes an observed 120us host stall in the trace.
- C: Force all attention kernels onto a single non-default stream to avoid implicit synchronizations -> reduced churn in CUPTI queueing and trimmed 30–70us.
- D: Coalesce tiny memcpy's into a single consolidated scatter using a batching window of 2–4 requests -> reduces amortized handshake but increases  tail correlation; tradeoff needs policy.

Microbench commands and example outputs (sanitized):
- cudaEvent measurement snippet:
  start = cudaEventRecord(e1, stream1)
  kernel<<<g,b,0,stream1>>>(...)
  cudaEventRecord(e2, stream1)
  cudaEventSynchronize(e2) // we used this in instrumentation only
  elapsed = cudaEventElapsedTime(e1,e2) // kernel time 0.85ms
  // but host timestamp delta(end_of_kernel, start_of_next_kernel) = 1.32ms -> handshake 0.47ms

- nvprof-like sample (trimmed):
  KernelA_fused         time  0.84ms  (stream 1)
  HostMemcpy_small      time  0.11ms  (host pinned)
  cuBLAS_gemm_blocking  time  0.14ms  (causes implicit sync)
  KernelB_paged         time  0.90ms  (stream 0)

Operational tradeoffs and options we considered:
1) Avoid mixed kernel handoffs inside a single request: prefer coarse-grained routing so each request hits a single attention implementation. Pros: eliminates handshake entirely. Cons: routing granularity may reduce efficiency (e.g., some tokens could have benefited from fused ops).
2) Make paged-attn path non-blocking and pre-allocate/retain workspace: removes blocking and host zero cost, but increases persistent memory footprint and complexity of lifecycle management.
3) Introduce an on-GPU scatter/coalesce kernel to avoid small host-mediated DMAs. Requires kernel development but potentially large win for small requests.
4) Micro-batching window to coalesce small memcpy and kernel starts: config knob with latency vs throughput tradeoff.

Recommended immediate fixes (short-term, low-risk):
- Change cuBLAS calls in paged-attn to async variants and use explicit cudaEvent fences in user code instead of relying on synchronous returns. (PR: pr/1378)
- Allocate and keep a persistent workspace buffer per-device for paged-attn and use cuMemsetAsync at launch instead of host zeroing. Add watchdog to reclaim low-usage buffers to control memory.
- Unify default streams for attention-related kernels or adopt per-request stream affinity to avoid cross-stream syncs.

Medium-term projects (Q1):
- Implement an on-GPU scatter/coalesce helper kernel and evaluate replacing host scatter logic. This should eliminate small host memcpy bursts and reduce handshake by ~100–200us in our microbench.
- Evaluate policy: coarse routing vs hybrid per-token decisions with a small batching window. Run perf experiments using production trace samples to estimate cost/benefit.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Quantify memory footprint cost for persistent paged-attn workspace across our instance types (A100-80, H100-80, and smaller GPUs).
- Measure handshake behaviour under multi-tenant noisy neighbor scenarios (GPU context switching effects).
- Investigate whether kernel fusion re-ordering (merge additional ops into fused kernel) yields a net win for small sequences without breaking numerical equivalence.
- Add a deterministic unit test for handshake detection into the trace harness so regression alerts fire when handshake > Xus for small-batch requests.

Action items (owners):
- Aisha: land cuBLAS async changes + add cuMemsetAsync persistent-workspace prototype (PR draft ready)
- Tomás: prototype on-GPU scatter kernel (spike) and microbench harness
- Mei: run production trace simulation comparing coarse-routing vs hybrid with batching window
- Jordan: add NVTX trace assertions to our CI perf regression job and hook RL-7890 to alerting

Appendix: notes on measurement pitfalls and gotchas:
- Avoid cudaEventSynchronize(e2) in production traces; it can hide real concurrency. Use non-blocking events when possible and sample host timestamps carefully.
- Small host->device pinned copies are often optimized differently by drivers; batch them at the host-side if possible.
- NVLink vs PCIe farm differences: on NVLink-connected GPUs the DMA cost is lower but the host CPU staging and blocking calls still dominate the handshake.

End of notebook.

Rough estimated wins if we implement recommended short-term fixes: median handshake drop ~220us, 95p reduced by ~150–300us on small-batch interactive traces.

Notes-to-self: keep this doc as a lightweight lab notebook; when we have stable numbers move a cleaned version to confluence for the PM/infra review.
